claim: Twenty participants (11 females; 9 males; mean age = 23.5) were recruited from the general population around University College London to participate in the study.
source: Twenty participants (11 females; 9 males; mean age = 23.5) were recruited from the general population around University College London to participate in the study.
evidence: Direct statement about participant demographics in the Methods section.

claim: This sample size was commensurate with previous studies similar in design (Boorman et al., 2016; Howard et al., 2015; Jocham et al., 2016).
source: This sample size was commensurate with previous studies similar in design (Boorman et al., 2016; Howard et al., 2015; Jocham et al., 2016).
evidence: Comparison to prior literature to justify sample size.

claim: Using an independent, unpublished data set, a power analysis found that this number of participants had 84% power to detect the desired neural effect in lOFC.
source: Using an independent, unpublished data set, we conducted a power analysis for the desire neural effect in lOFC. We found that this number of participants had 84% power to detect this effect (see Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Power analysis conducted on independent dataset, results shown in supplementary figure.

claim: None of the participants reported a history of neurological or psychiatric disorder.
source: None of the participants reported a history of neurological or psychiatric disorder.
evidence: Direct statement about participant exclusion criteria.

claim: All participants spoke fluent English and had normal or corrected-to-normal vision.
source: All participants spoke fluent English and had normal or corrected-to-normal vision.
evidence: Direct statement about participant inclusion criteria.

claim: The study was approved by the UCL Research Ethics Committee (Project ID Number: 3450/002).
source: The study was approved by the UCL Research Ethics Committee (Project ID Number: 3450/002), and all participants gave written informed consent.

claim: All participants gave written informed consent.
source: The study was approved by the UCL Research Ethics Committee (Project ID Number: 3450/002), and all participants gave written informed consent.
evidence: Direct statement about informed consent procedure.

claim: Participants completed a learning task in which they tracked associations between abstract shapes and specific reward identities (gift cards to two different stores), which were rated for approximately equal desirability.
source: Participants completed a learning task in which they tracked associations between abstract shapes and specific reward identities (gift cards to two different stores), which were rated for approximately equal desirability.
evidence: Direct description of the task design.

claim: In each trial, participants selected one of two abstract shapes, which were randomly presented on either the left or right side of the screen.
source: In each trial, participants selected one of two abstract shapes, which were randomly presented on either the left or right side of the screen.

claim: Decisions were based on two pieces of information: (1) inferred estimates of the probability that a particular shape would lead to each gift card based on the history of previous trials, and (2) the point value of each gift card on the current trial.
source: Decisions were based on two pieces of information: (1) inferred estimates of the probability that a particular shape would lead to each gift card based on the history of previous trials, and (2) the point value of each gift card on the current trial (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: Direct description of decision-making factors, illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Participants were informed prior to starting the task that one of the trials would be chosen at random to count 'for real' at the end of the experiment.
source: Participants were informed prior to starting the task that one of the trials would be chosen at random to count 'for real' at the end of the experiment.

claim: For the randomly selected trial, participants would receive money on the awarded gift card that was commensurate with the number of associated points (number of points divided by four).
source: For this trial, they would receive money on the awarded gift card that was commensurate with the number of associated points (number of points divided by four).

claim: Point values for each outcome were presented as two numbers at the top of the screen, with the color of each number indicating the associated gift card identity.
source: Point values for each outcome were presented as two numbers at the top of the screen, with the color of each number indicating the associated gift card identity.

claim: The position of the numbers relative to each other (top or bottom) was determined randomly on each trial.
source: Their position relative to each other (top or bottom) was determined randomly on each trial.

claim: Each shape had a specific probability of leading to each outcome and an inverse probability of leading to the other outcome.
source: Each shape had a specific probability of leading to each outcome and an inverse probability of leading to the other outcome.

claim: The true probabilities would drift independently over the course of the experiment, meaning that information about outcome probabilities could not be shared across shapes.
source: These true probabilities would drift independently over the course of the experiment, meaning that information about outcome probabilities could not be shared across shapes.

claim: On any given trial, the number of points that could be won for each gift card ranged from 20 to 100, with a minimum difference of at least 15 points.
source: On any given trial, the number of points that could be won for each gift card ranged from 20 to 100, with a minimum difference of at least 15 points.
evidence: Direct statement about reward magnitude parameters.

claim: Although reward magnitudes were predetermined, participants were told they were randomly generated at the beginning of each trial and that it was not useful to track them.
source: Although these magnitudes were predetermined, participants were told they were randomly generated at the beginning of each trial and that it was not useful to track them (Pearson correlation between magnitudes in trial n and n+1 was less than.2).
evidence: Direct statement about instructions and correlation analysis.

claim: The Pearson correlation between magnitudes in trial n and n+1 was less than 0.2.
source: Although these magnitudes were predetermined, participants were told they were randomly generated at the beginning of each trial and that it was not useful to track them (Pearson correlation between magnitudes in trial n and n+1 was less than.2).
evidence: Statistical analysis of reward magnitude correlations.

claim: To maximize rewards, participants had to track the probability that a shape led to each outcome and combine this with the reward magnitudes associated with each outcome on the current trial.
source: Instead, to maximize rewards, participants had to track the probability that a shape led to each outcome and combine this with the reward magnitudes associated with each outcome on the current trial.

claim: Each trial began with viewing the two possible choices for 0.5 s, during which selection was not possible.
source: Each trial began with viewing the two possible choices for 0.5 s, during which selection was not possible.

claim: Participants had 3.5 s to make their selection between the two options.
source: They then had 3.5 s to make their selection between the two options.

claim: The selected shape was highlighted for 0.5 s before proceeding to the interstimulus interval (ISI).
source: The selected shape was highlighted for 0.5 s, before proceeding to the interstimulus interval (ISI), which lasted for a randomly selected duration between 4 s and 8 s.

claim: The interstimulus interval (ISI) lasted for a randomly selected duration between 4 s and 8 s.
source: The selected shape was highlighted for 0.5 s, before proceeding to the interstimulus interval (ISI), which lasted for a randomly selected duration between 4 s and 8 s.

claim: The outcome was presented for 2000ms before a jittered inter-trial-interval (ITI) of 4s to 8s.
source: The outcome was then presented for 2000ms before a jittered inter-trial-interval (ITI) of 4s to 8s.

claim: Participants did not have any prior knowledge about choice-outcome associations or how quickly these associations might change.
source: Participants did not have any prior knowledge about choice-outcome associations or how quickly these associations might change, but they knew that they could change throughout the task.

claim: Participants knew that choice-outcome associations could change throughout the task.
source: Participants did not have any prior knowledge about choice-outcome associations or how quickly these associations might change, but they knew that they could change throughout the task.

claim: Participants needed to infer both the current associative contingency for each shape and when these contingencies changed from their history of choices and observed outcomes.
source: Therefore, participants needed to infer both the current associative contingency for each shape and when these contingencies changed from their history of choices and observed outcomes.

claim: Each run of the scanning session began with a 'template task' in which participants passively viewed a sequence of all four stimuli (two shapes and two gift cards), individually presented in random order.
source: Each run of the scanning session began with a 'template task'. In this task, participants passively viewed a sequence of all four stimuli (two shapes and two gift cards), individually presented in random order.

claim: To ensure that participants were paying attention during passive viewing, they were presented with four 'catch trials' which occurred at random between images.
source: To ensure that participants were paying attention during passive viewing, they were presented with four 'catch trials' which occurred at random between images (see Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Direct statement about attention checks, illustrated in supplementary figure.

claim: In catch trials, all four stimuli were presented simultaneously, and participants were asked to indicate which stimulus had just been presented.
source: In catch trials, all four stimuli were presented simultaneously, and participants were asked to indicate which stimulus had just been presented (see Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Direct description of catch trial procedure, illustrated in supplementary figure.

claim: Participants were told they could earn an additional £10 on the selected gift card if they responded correctly to catch trials.
source: Participants were told they could earn an additional £10 on the selected gift card if they responded correctly.

claim: Participants would be deducted £1 for each incorrect response or for not making responses in time (max response time = 3 s) on catch trials.
source: However, they would be deducted £1 for each incorrect response or for not making responses in time (max response time = 3 s).

claim: Average accuracy for catch trials was generally high (mean = 0.75, std = 0.15).
source: Average accuracy for these catch trials was generally high (mean = 0.75, std = 0.15).
evidence: Statistical summary of catch trial performance.

claim: Participants viewed each item in the template task for 1 s followed by a 2.5 s ISI.
source: Participants viewed each item for 1 s followed by a 2.5 s ISI.
evidence: Direct description of template task timing.

claim: Two visually distinct abstract shapes were used as choice objects, randomly assigned to serve as S1 or S2 for each participant.
source: Two visually distinct abstract shapes were used as choice objects. These shapes were randomly assigned to serve as S1 or S2 for each participant.

claim: The two gift cards were chosen to serve as reward identities from six different possible gift cards (iTunes, Argos, Blackwells, Marks & Spencers, Boots, and Starbucks).
source: The two gift cards were chosen to serve as reward identities during the experiment from six different possible gift cards (iTunes, Argos, Blackwells, Marks & Spencers, Boots, and Starbucks).

claim: Each participant rated the six gift cards on a scale from 0 (not preferable) to 100 (extremely preferable).
source: Each participant rated the six gift cards on a scale from 0 (not preferable) to 100 (extremely preferable).

claim: The two gift cards were selected to have the minimal difference in ratings among the highest rated gift cards to prevent a strong preference for one outcome over the other.
source: The two gift cards were selected to have the minimal difference in ratings among the highest rated gift cards. This was done to prevent a strong preference for one outcome over the other.
evidence: Direct statement about selection criteria and rationale.

claim: All stimuli were presented on a computer running Presentation software (Version 18.1).
source: All stimuli were presented on a computer running Presentation software (Version 18.1, https://www.neurobs.com/).

claim: A reward schedule was generated that predetermined the outcome obtained for each choice on each trial, but this schedule was unknown to the participants.
source: We generated a reward schedule that predetermined the outcome obtained for each choice on each trial, but this schedule was unknown to the participants.

claim: The schedule was optimized such that an ideal Bayesian learner would choose each shape and receive each outcome approximately an equal number of times.
source: We optimized the schedule such that an ideal Bayesian learner (see Bayesian Computational model) would choose each shape and receive each outcome approximately an equal number of times (percent of overall trials where S1 was chosen was between 42% and 57%).
evidence: Direct statement about schedule optimization with reference to computational model.

claim: The percent of overall trials where S1 was chosen was between 42% and 57%.
source: We optimized the schedule such that an ideal Bayesian learner (see Bayesian Computational model) would choose each shape and receive each outcome approximately an equal number of times (percent of overall trials where S1 was chosen was between 42% and 57%).

claim: Schedule optimization was done to reduce the potential for sampling bias in planned multivariate analyses.
source: This was done to reduce the potential for sampling bias in planned multivariate analyses.

claim: The schedule of outcomes for each shape was generated with independently drifting probabilities so participants could not learn anything about one shape from observing the outcome of the other shape.
source: The schedule of outcomes for each shape was generated with independently drifting probabilities so participants could not learn anything about one shape from observing the outcome of the other shape (see Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Direct statement about task structure, illustrated in supplementary figure.

claim: Participants completed three scanning runs in one session.
source: Participants completed three scanning runs in one session.

claim: The first two runs began with the template task, which was followed by the learning task (37 trials of the direct transition condition, then 37 trials of the indirect transition condition).
source: The first two runs began with the template task, which was followed by the learning task (37 trials of the direct transition condition, then 37 trials of the indirect transition condition).

claim: The third run consisted of only the template task.
source: The third run consisted of only the template task.

claim: The learning task began with instructions stating 'Your latest choice', indicating that participants were in the direct transition condition.
source: The learning task began with instructions stating, 'Your latest choice', indicating that participants were in the direct transition condition.

claim: After 37 trials, a second instruction screen showed 'Your previous choice' indicating that participants were about to start the indirect transition condition.
source: After 37 trials, a second instruction screen showed 'Your previous choice' indicating that participants were about the start indirect transition condition.

claim: Participants knew that in the indirect transition condition, the first outcome observed was not linked to any choice.
source: Participants knew that in the indirect transition condition, the first outcome observed was not linked to any choice.

claim: In each run, three 'bonus trials' were included (two in the direct transition condition and one in the indirect transition condition), distributed throughout choice trials, which occurred between a choice and the outcome.
source: In each run, we included three 'bonus trials' (two in the direct transition condition and one in the indirect transition condition), distributed throughout choice trials, which occurred between a choice and the outcome.
evidence: Direct description of bonus trial distribution.

claim: In bonus trials, participants were shown the two gift cards on either side of a question mark and were given the chance to predict which outcome they would receive in the upcoming feedback period.
source: Participants were shown the two gift cards on either side of a question mark and were given the chance to predict which outcome they would receive in the upcoming feedback period.
evidence: Direct description of bonus trial procedure.

claim: For each correct gift card prediction in bonus trials, participants received an additional £3 on the gift card they would receive at the end.
source: For each correct gift card prediction, they received an additional £3 on the gift card they would receive at the end.

claim: Prior to each scanning session, participants completed a shortened (76 trials) behavioral training session.
source: Prior to each scanning session, participants completed a shortened (76 trials) behavioral training session.

claim: In the training session, participants completed a practice version of the choice task, which had a unique reward schedule.
source: In the training session, participants completed a practice version of the choice task, which had a unique reward schedule.

claim: Prior to the practice trials, participants were verbally given a 'comprehension quiz' to verify they understood key elements of the task, such as the difference between choice-outcome transitions in each condition.
source: Prior to the practice trials, participants were verbally given a 'comprehension quiz' to verify they understood key elements of the task, such as the difference between choice-outcome transitions in each condition.

claim: The distribution of ISI and ITI durations for the training session was constrained to 2s to 4s.
source: Finally, the distribution of ISI and ITI durations for this session was constrained to 2s to 4s.
evidence: Direct statement about training session timing.

claim: Brain images were acquired using a 32-channel head coil from a 3 Tesla Siemens Trio scanner.
source: The brain images were acquired using a 32-channel head coil from a 3 Tesla Siemens Trio scanner.

claim: A T2*-weighted echo-planar imaging (EPI) sequence was used to collect 43 2 mm slices in ascending order, with 1 mm gaps.
source: We used a T2*-weighted echo-planar imaging (EPI) sequence to collect 43 2 mm slices in ascending order, with 1 mm gaps.

claim: The in-plane resolution was 3x3 mm, with a repetition time (TR) of 3.01 s and echo-time (TE) of 70ms.
source: The in-plane resolution was of 3x3 mm, with a repetition time (TR) of 3.01 s and echo-time (TE) of 70ms.

claim: The slice angle was set to a 30 degree tilt relative to the rostro-caudal axis to minimize signal loss from the lOFC (Weiskopf et al., 2006).
source: We set the slice angle to a 30 degree tilt relative to the rostro-caudal axis to minimize signal loss from the lOFC (Weiskopf et al., 2006) and applied a local z-shim with a moment of –0.4 mT/m to the OFC.
evidence: Direct description of imaging parameters with citation supporting the rationale.

claim: A local z-shim with a moment of –0.4 mT/m was applied to the OFC.
source: We set the slice angle to a 30 degree tilt relative to the rostro-caudal axis to minimize signal loss from the lOFC (Weiskopf et al., 2006) and applied a local z-shim with a moment of –0.4 mT/m to the OFC.

claim: The first five volumes of each block were discarded to allow for T1 equilibration effects.
source: The first five volumes of each block were discarded to allow for T1 equilibration effects.

claim: For accurate registration of the EPI to a standard space, a T1-weighted anatomical scan was acquired with a magnetization-prepared rapid gradient echo sequence (MPRAGE) with a 1×1 × 1 mm resolution.
source: For accurate registration of the EPI to a standard space, we acquired a T1-weighted anatomical scan with a magnetization-prepared rapid gradient echo sequence (MPRAGE) with a 1×1 × 1 mm resolution.

claim: To measure and correct for geometric distortions due to susceptibility-induced field inhomogeneities, a whole-brain field map with dual echo-time images (TE1=10ms, TE2=14.76ms, resolution 3×3 × 3 mm) was acquired.
source: Finally, to measure and correct for geometric distortions due to susceptibility-induced field inhomogeneities, a whole-brain field map with dual echo-time images (TE1=10ms, TE2=14.76ms, resolution 3×3 × 3 mm) was also acquired.
evidence: Direct description of field map acquisition.

claim: Slice time correction was performed on functional scans.
source: We performed slice time correction, corrected for signal bias, and realigned functional scans to the first volume in the sequence using a six-parameter rigid body transformation to correct for motion.

claim: Signal bias correction was performed on functional scans.
source: We performed slice time correction, corrected for signal bias, and realigned functional scans to the first volume in the sequence using a six-parameter rigid body transformation to correct for motion.

claim: Functional scans were realigned to the first volume in the sequence using a six-parameter rigid body transformation to correct for motion.
source: We performed slice time correction, corrected for signal bias, and realigned functional scans to the first volume in the sequence using a six-parameter rigid body transformation to correct for motion.
evidence: Direct description of motion correction procedure.

claim: Images were spatially normalized by warping participant-specific images to the reference brain in the MNI (Montreal Neurological Institute) reference brain.
source: Images were then spatially normalized by warping participant-specific images to the reference brain in the MNI (Montreal Neurological Institute) reference brain and smoothed using an 8 mm full-width at half maximum Gaussian kernel.

claim: Images were smoothed using an 8 mm full-width at half maximum Gaussian kernel.
source: Images were then spatially normalized by warping participant-specific images to the reference brain in the MNI (Montreal Neurological Institute) reference brain and smoothed using an 8 mm full-width at half maximum Gaussian kernel.

claim: Pre-processing was done in SPM12 using Matlab 2018a.
source: Pre-processing was done in SPM12 (Wellcome Trust Centre for Neuroimaging, http://www.fil.ion.ucl.ac.uk/spm) using Matlab 2018a.

claim: The mean of the β-values which reflect appropriate credit assignment in each condition were significantly higher than the mean β-values which represented credit spreading (direct transition condition: t(19) = 5.39, p<0.001, indirect transition condition: t(19) = 4.34, p<0.001).
source: Furthermore, the mean of the β-values which reflect appropriate credit assignment in each condition were significantly higher than the mean β-values which represented credit spreading (direct transition condition: t(19) = 5.39, p<0.001, indirect transition condition: t(19) = 4.34, p<0.001; Figure 1E and F).
evidence: Statistical comparison results shown in text and Figures 1E and F.

claim: Participants used the appropriate task-structure when assigning credit for observed outcomes in each condition.
source: These results show that participants used the appropriate task-structure when assigning credit for observed outcomes in each condition.

claim: Follow-up analysis showed that participants' choices in each trial integrated expectations about the probability of receiving a particular outcome and its magnitude and did not rely on estimates of a cached option value.
source: Follow-up analysis showed that participants' choices in each trial integrated expectations about the probability of receiving a particular outcome and its magnitude and did not rely on estimates of a cached option value (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Results of follow-up analysis shown in supplementary figure.

claim: β-values representing appropriate credit assignment in the direct transition condition were higher than those in the indirect transition condition (t(19) = 1.81, p<0.05).
source: We found that β-values representing appropriate credit assignment in the direct transition condition were higher than those in the indirect transition condition (t(19) = 1.81, p<0.05).

claim: β-values in cells that represent credit spreading in the direct transition condition were not significantly lower than those in the indirect transition condition (t(19) = 1.11, p=0.14).
source: However, β-values in cells that represent credit spreading in the direct transition condition were not significantly lower than those in the indirect transition condition (t(19) = 1.11, p=0.14).

claim: Credit assignment was less precise in the indirect transition condition compared to the direct transition condition, despite each being appropriate for the respective task structure overall.
source: These results indicate that credit assignment was less precise in the indirect transition condition compared to the direct transition condition, despite each being appropriate for the respective task structure overall.

claim: Significant decoding of the causal choice was found in left lOFC ([x,y,z] = [–26, 42,–8], t(19) = 4.22, pTFCE <0.05 ROI-corrected) in the direct transition condition.
source: Specifically, we found significant and marginally significant decoding of the causal choice in left ([x,y,z] = [–26, 42,–8], t(19) = 4.22, pTFCE <0.05 ROI-corrected using threshold-free cluster enhancement (TFCE) correction Smith and Nichols, 2009) and right ([x,y,z] = [24, 46, -8], t(19) = 3.45, pTFCE = 0.081 ROI-corrected) lOFC, respectively (Figure 2A).
evidence: MVPA decoding results with statistical correction, shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Marginally significant decoding of the causal choice was found in right lOFC ([x,y,z] = [24, 46, -8], t(19) = 3.45, pTFCE = 0.081 ROI-corrected) in the direct transition condition.
source: Specifically, we found significant and marginally significant decoding of the causal choice in left ([x,y,z] = [–26, 42,–8], t(19) = 4.22, pTFCE <0.05 ROI-corrected using threshold-free cluster enhancement (TFCE) correction Smith and Nichols, 2009) and right ([x,y,z] = [24, 46, -8], t(19) = 3.45, pTFCE = 0.081 ROI-corrected) lOFC, respectively (Figure 2A).
evidence: MVPA decoding results with statistical correction, shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Right HC showed significant decoding of the causal choice ([x,y,z] = [36, -20, -16], t(19) = 4.02, pTFCE <0.05 ROI-corrected) in the direct transition condition.
source: A similar pattern was also apparent in the HC, where right HC showed significant decoding ([x,y,z] = [36, -20, -16], t(19) = 4.02, pTFCE <0.05 ROI-corrected), while left HC showed a marginal effect ([x,y,z] = [-22,–10, –24], t(19) = 2.86, pTFCE = 0.080 ROI-corrected).
evidence: MVPA decoding results with statistical correction.

claim: Left HC showed a marginal effect for decoding the causal choice ([x,y,z] = [-22,–10, –24], t(19) = 2.86, pTFCE = 0.080 ROI-corrected) in the direct transition condition.
source: A similar pattern was also apparent in the HC, where right HC showed significant decoding ([x,y,z] = [36, -20, -16], t(19) = 4.02, pTFCE <0.05 ROI-corrected), while left HC showed a marginal effect ([x,y,z] = [-22,–10, –24], t(19) = 2.86, pTFCE = 0.080 ROI-corrected).
evidence: MVPA decoding results with statistical correction.

claim: The lOFC and HC represent the causal choice at the time when credit is assigned in the direct condition.
source: Together, these results show that the lOFC and HC represent the causal choice at the time when credit is assigned in the direct condition of our task.

claim: Repeating the causal choice decoding analysis on the indirect transition condition did not reveal a significant effect in any a priori defined ROI (all pTFCE >0.05 ROI corrected).
source: Repeating the causal choice decoding analysis on this condition did not reveal a significant effect in any a priori defined ROI (all pTFCE >0.05 ROI corrected), nor did we find significant decoding elsewhere in the brain (all pTFCE >0.05 whole brain corrected).

claim: No significant decoding of the causal choice was found elsewhere in the brain in the indirect transition condition (all pTFCE >0.05 whole brain corrected).
source: Repeating the causal choice decoding analysis on this condition did not reveal a significant effect in any a priori defined ROI (all pTFCE >0.05 ROI corrected), nor did we find significant decoding elsewhere in the brain (all pTFCE >0.05 whole brain corrected).
evidence: Null result from whole-brain MVPA analysis.

claim: A cluster of voxels specifically within the right lFPC ([x,y,z] = (28, 54, 8), t(19) = 3.74, pTFCE <0.05 ROI-corrected) showed significant decoding of the pending causal choice at feedback time.
source: Our analysis revealed a cluster of voxels specifically within the right lFPC ([x,y,z] = (28, 54, 8), t(19) = 3.74, pTFCE <0.05 ROI-corrected; left hemisphere all pTFCE >0.1, Figure 3A), consistent with right lFPC coding for the pending causal choice at feedback time, precisely when the outcome of the prior choice causal choice needed to be evaluated.
evidence: MVPA decoding results with statistical correction, shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Left hemisphere lFPC did not show significant decoding of the pending causal choice (all pTFCE >0.1).
source: Our analysis revealed a cluster of voxels specifically within the right lFPC ([x,y,z] = (28, 54, 8), t(19) = 3.74, pTFCE <0.05 ROI-corrected; left hemisphere all pTFCE >0.1, Figure 3A), consistent with right lFPC coding for the pending causal choice at feedback time, precisely when the outcome of the prior choice causal choice needed to be evaluated.
evidence: Null result from MVPA analysis in left lFPC.

claim: Right lFPC codes for the pending causal choice at feedback time, precisely when the outcome of the prior causal choice needed to be evaluated.
source: Our analysis revealed a cluster of voxels specifically within the right lFPC ([x,y,z] = (28, 54, 8), t(19) = 3.74, pTFCE <0.05 ROI-corrected; left hemisphere all pTFCE >0.1, Figure 3A), consistent with right lFPC coding for the pending causal choice at feedback time, precisely when the outcome of the prior choice causal choice needed to be evaluated.

claim: Information connectivity analysis revealed strong IC between representations in lFPC at feedback on trial t and the representations in lOFC and HC during feedback on trial t+1.
source: This analysis revealed strong IC between representations in lFPC at feedback on trial t and the representations in lOFC and HC during feedback on trial t+1.

claim: Significant correlations in decoding distance were found between lFPC and bilateral lOFC ([x,y,z] = [-32,24,–22], t(19) = 3.81, [x,y,z] = [20, 38, -14], t(19) = 3.87, pTFCE <0.05 ROI corrected).
source: Specifically, we found significant correlations in decoding distance between lFPC and bilateral lOFC ([x,y,z] = [-32,24,–22], t(19) = 3.81, [x,y,z] = [20, 38, -14], t(19) = 3.87, pTFCE <0.05 ROI corrected) and bilateral HC ([x,y,z] = [-28,–10, –24], t(19) = 3.41, [x,y,z] = [22, -10, -24], t(19) = 4.21, pTFCE <0.05 ROI corrected), Figure 3C.
evidence: Information connectivity analysis results with statistical correction, shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Significant correlations in decoding distance were found between lFPC and bilateral HC ([x,y,z] = [-28,–10, –24], t(19) = 3.41, [x,y,z] = [22, -10, -24], t(19) = 4.21, pTFCE <0.05 ROI corrected).
source: Specifically, we found significant correlations in decoding distance between lFPC and bilateral lOFC ([x,y,z] = [-32,24,–22], t(19) = 3.81, [x,y,z] = [20, 38, -14], t(19) = 3.87, pTFCE <0.05 ROI corrected) and bilateral HC ([x,y,z] = [-28,–10, –24], t(19) = 3.41, [x,y,z] = [22, -10, -24], t(19) = 4.21, pTFCE <0.05 ROI corrected), Figure 3C.
evidence: Information connectivity analysis results with statistical correction, shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Subsequent analyses confirmed that the information connectivity effect was due to these regions showing a significant increase in positive (correct) decoding in trials where pending information could be positively (correctly) decoded in lFPC, and not simply due to a reduction in incorrect information fidelity.
source: Subsequent analyses confirmed that this effect was due to these regions showing a significant increase in positive (correct) decoding in trials where pending information could be positively (correctly) decoded in lFPC, and not simply due to a reduction in incorrect information fidelity (see Figure 3C and D).
evidence: Results of control analyses shown in Figures 3C and D.

claim: The coding of the causal choice during feedback in lOFC and HC is dependent on that causal choice being faithfully maintained in a pending state in the lFPC.
source: This finding is consistent with the coding of the causal choice during feedback in lOFC and HC being dependent on that causal choice being faithfully maintained in a pending state in the lFPC.

claim: Significant decoding of the causal stimulus identity at the time of feedback when averaged across direct and indirect conditions was found in the left HC ([x,y,z] = [-26,–16, –16], t(19) = 5.20, pTFCE <0.001 ROI-corrected).
source: This revealed significant decoding of the causal stimulus identity at the time of feedback when averaged across direct and indirect conditions, in the left HC (Figure 4A; [x,y,z] = [-26,–16, –16], t(19) = 5.20, pTFCE <0.001 ROI-corrected; right hemisphere all pTFCE >0.1).
evidence: MVPA decoding results with statistical correction, shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Right hemisphere HC did not show significant decoding of causal stimulus identity (all pTFCE >0.1).
source: This revealed significant decoding of the causal stimulus identity at the time of feedback when averaged across direct and indirect conditions, in the left HC (Figure 4A; [x,y,z] = [-26,–16, –16], t(19) = 5.20, pTFCE <0.001 ROI-corrected; right hemisphere all pTFCE >0.1).
evidence: Null result from MVPA analysis in right HC.
